ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Ethics approval was obtained from the Macquarie University Human Ethics Committee (Ref: 5201600387 and 5201700825).
Participants were selected from the Macquarie University Motor Neuron Disease (MND) Research Centre's Neurodegenerative Disease Biobank.

All participants with ALS received a probable or definite diagnosis according to the revised El Escorial criteria [19], as determined by a consultant neurologist; eligible participants were aged 18 years or older and provided written informed consent or where the participant lacked capacity, consent via a legally authorised representative.
table.formatted: All participants with ALS received a probable or definite diagnosis according to the revised El Escorial criteria <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>, as determined by a consultant neurologist; eligible participants were aged 18 years or older and provided written informed consent or where the participant lacked capacity, consent via a legally authorised representative.

table.text: Unaffected controls (hereafter referred to as healthy controls) without a diagnosis of ALS or another neurodegenerative disease were recruited in parallel through the same biobank; body mass index was not routinely collected for controls.

Functional impairment was monitored using the ALSFRS-R. Across the longitudinal ALS group, participants had a median of 3 visits (IQR: 2 to 4) over a median follow-up duration of 1.48 years (IQR: 0.69-2.28), with a median inter-visit interval of 0.5 years (IQR: 0.36-0.95) (Figure 1).

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Participants were selected from the Macquarie University Motor Neuron Disease (MND) Research Centre's Neurodegenerative Disease Biobank.

> All participants with ALS received a probable or definite diagnosis according to the revised El Escorial criteria [19], as determined by a consultant neurologist; eligible participants were aged 18 years or older and provided written informed consent or where the participant lacked capacity, consent via a legally authorised representative.

> Unaffected controls (hereafter referred to as healthy controls) without a diagnosis of ALS or another neurodegenerative disease were recruited in parallel through the same biobank; body mass index was not routinely collected for controls.

> Functional impairment was monitored using the ALSFRS-R. Across the longitudinal ALS group, participants had a median of 3 visits (IQR: 2 to 4) over a median follow-up duration of 1.48 years (IQR: 0.69-2.28), with a median inter-visit interval of 0.5 years (IQR: 0.36-0.95) (Figure 1).

Ethics approval statement:

> Ethics approval was obtained from the Macquarie University Human Ethics Committee (Ref: 5201600387 and 5201700825).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.header: Prospective Association Between IGF-1 and Short-Term Functional Change
table.expanded: In the primary model adjusted for inter-visit interval, baseline BMI, age and sex, every 1 SD higher IGF-1 concentration at the prior visit was associated with a 1.40-point higher subsequent ΔALSFRS-R (95% CI 0.03 to 2.77, p = 0.045), implying less functional decline at the next follow-up visit.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p < 0.05", Text = "All statistical tests were two-tailed with statistical significance defined nominally as p < 0.05 for the prespecified primary normal approximation analysis."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

summary_table.ethics_statements: Ethics approval was obtained from the Macquarie University Human Ethics Committee (Ref: 5201600387 and 5201700825).
live_data_statements: Participants were selected from the Macquarie University Motor Neuron Disease (MND) Research Centre's Neurodegenerative Disease Biobank.

All participants with ALS received a probable or definite diagnosis according to the revised El Escorial criteria [19], as determined by a consultant neurologist; eligible participants were aged 18 years or older and provided written informed consent or where the participant lacked capacity, consent via a legally authorised representative.

Unaffected controls (hereafter referred to as healthy controls) without a diagnosis of ALS or another neurodegenerative disease were recruited in parallel through the same biobank; body mass index was not routinely collected for controls.

Functional impairment was monitored using the ALSFRS-R. Across the longitudinal ALS group, participants had a median of 3 visits (IQR: 2 to 4) over a median follow-up duration of 1.48 years (IQR: 0.69-2.28), with a median inter-visit interval of 0.5 years (IQR: 0.36-0.95) (Figure 1).
